---
title: "Continuous variation from many loci"
description: "How many genes of small effect plus environmental noise produce a smooth, bell-shaped distribution."
---

## The idea

Mendel's traits fall into distinct classes, yet most traits breeders care about (yield, height, maturity) vary continuously. Falconer & Mackay reconcile the two: a metric trait is influenced by many loci, each with a small effect, and by environmental variation. With one locus an F~2~ shows three genotype classes. With more loci the number of classes grows, adjacent classes differ by less, and environmental noise blurs them into a continuous, approximately normal distribution.

For *n* unlinked additive loci, each segregating 1:2:1 in an F~2~ with effect *a* per allele, the genotypic values follow a binomial distribution with 2*n* + 1 classes and variance

$$
V_G = n \cdot \tfrac{1}{2} a^2 .
$$

In the widget the per-allele effect is scaled to *a* = √(2/*n*), so *V*~G~ stays at 1 as *n* changes. Environmental variance is set from the heritability: *V*~E~ = *V*~G~ (1 − *h*²) / *h*².

*Source: Falconer & Mackay, chapter 6.*

## Widget

```{ojs}
import {pal, rng, normal} from "../js/common.js"

viewof nLoci = Inputs.range([1, 50], {value: 1, step: 1, label: "Segregating loci (n)"})
viewof h2 = Inputs.range([0.05, 1], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "Heritability (h²)"})
viewof nPlants = Inputs.range([200, 5000], {value: 2000, step: 100, label: "F₂ plants"})
```

```{ojs}
plants = {
  const u = rng(12345 + nLoci * 31 + nPlants);
  const z = normal(u);
  const a = Math.sqrt(2 / nLoci);
  const sdE = h2 >= 1 ? 0 : Math.sqrt((1 - h2) / h2);
  return d3.range(nPlants).map(() => {
    let g = 0;
    for (let l = 0; l < nLoci; l++) g += (u() < 0.5) + (u() < 0.5) - 1;
    const G = g * a;
    return {G, P: G + sdE * z()};
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  height: 320,
  marginLeft: 50,
  x: {label: "Phenotype (standardized units)"},
  y: {label: "Plants", grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectY(plants, Plot.binX({y: "count"}, {x: "P", thresholds: 60, fill: pal[0], inset: 1, tip: true})),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
md`Genotype classes possible: **${2 * nLoci + 1}**. Observed phenotypic variance: **${d3.variance(plants, d => d.P).toFixed(2)}** (genetic ≈ 1, environmental ≈ ${(h2 >= 1 ? 0 : (1 - h2) / h2).toFixed(2)}).`
```

## Things to try

- Start at *n* = 1 and *h*² = 1. You see three spikes in a 1:2:1 ratio. Raise *n* to 2, 3 and 5 and watch the classes multiply.
- Keep *n* = 1 but lower *h*² to 0.3. Environmental noise alone can make a single-gene trait look continuous.
- Set *n* = 20 and *h*² = 1. Even with no environmental variance the distribution is already close to normal.
